title: Adding servers, and why it is late
summary: Autoscaling adds servers when busy, but new servers take minutes to start.

steps.title: More servers on demand
steps.text: Evening traffic is much heavier than the dead of night. Instead of paying for peak servers all day, autoscaling adds servers when they are busy and removes them when quiet.

steps.prompt: Evening rush and a viral spike are coming. Turn on Autoscale for the servers.
steps.hint: Select the servers, switch Autoscale on, and set the highest number to 20 with a target of 60 percent.

steps.title: Why it is always a little late
steps.text: Reacting to a spike leaves a gap before new capacity is ready. Compare that gap with servers prepared in advance.

steps.q: Why not run peak servers all day?
choices: Servers wear out faster when always on
You pay for servers that sit idle
The law limits server running hours
Peak servers are slower at night
steps.why: Autoscaling saves money in quiet hours.

steps.q: Why can a spike still break an autoscaled system?
choices: Autoscaling is switched off after dark
Servers cannot be added during a spike
New servers need minutes to start up
The load balancer refuses extra servers
steps.why: The spike can outrun the startup time.

steps.q: A famous launch is at noon. Best move?
choices: Wait and let autoscaling react to it
Turn off the cache to save money now
Ask users to come back a bit later
Add servers a little before noon
steps.why: When you know the time, scale ahead of it.

takeaway: Autoscaling follows the crowd; for known surges, scale ahead of it.
